## Parametric Bootstrap Test

Let $S_i \in \mathbb{R}^{\binom{p}{2}}$ denote the vector of ECE terms across all pairs at index $i$, so that $\bar{S}_j = \hat\sigma_{x_j y_j}$ for each pair $j$. To test $H_0$, we need the variance of $\bar{S} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n S_i$.

Since $S_i$ depends only on observations at indices $i, i+1, i+2$, terms separated by 3 or more indices are independent. The variance therefore has bandwidth 2:
\begin{align*}
\operatorname{Var}\!\left(\bar{S}\right) &= \frac{1}{n^2}\left(\sum_{i=1}^n \operatorname{Var}(S_i) + \sum_{i=1}^n\bigl[\operatorname{Cov}(S_i, S_{i+1}) + \operatorname{Cov}(S_{i+1}, S_i)\bigr]\right. \\
&\quad\left. + \sum_{i=1}^n\bigl[\operatorname{Cov}(S_i, S_{i+2}) + \operatorname{Cov}(S_{i+2}, S_i)\bigr]\right).
\end{align*}
Plugging in $\operatorname{Var}(S_i) = \mathbb{E}[S_i S_i^\top]$ and $\operatorname{Cov}(S_i, S_{i+k}) = \mathbb{E}[S_i S_{i+k}^\top]$ and estimating by sample quantities gives
$$V := \widehat{\operatorname{Var}}\!\left(\bar{S}\right) = \frac{1}{n^2}\left(\sum_{i=1}^n S_i S_i^\top + \sum_{i=1}^{n}\!\left(S_i S_{i+1}^\top + S_{i+1} S_i^\top\right) + \sum_{i=1}^{n}\!\left(S_i S_{i+2}^\top + S_{i+2} S_i^\top\right)\right).$$

Writing $S \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times q}$ for the matrix with rows $S_i^\top$, and letting $C_k$ denote the cyclic shift matrix so that $C_k S$ has rows $S_{i+k}^\top$, this can be written compactly as
$$V = \frac{1}{n^2} S^\top \left(I + C_1 + C_1^\top + C_2 + C_2^\top\right) S.$$

**Parametric Bootstrap Test.** Under $H_0$, $\bar{S} \approx N(0, V)$ by the CLT. This gives a direct procedure:

1. Compute the observed statistic $T_\text{obs} = \max_{1 \leq j \leq p} |\bar{S}_j|$.
2. Draw $S^{(b)} \sim N(0, V)$ for $b = 1, \ldots, B$.
3. Compute $T^{(b)} = \max_{1 \leq j \leq p} |S^{(b)}_j|$.
4. The p-value is $\frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^B \mathbf{1}\!\left[T^{(b)} \geq T_\text{obs}\right]$.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Code: Parametric Bootstrap P-values are Uniform Under $H_0$
```{R}
#| cache: true
config <- scenario(2, n = 1000, L = 2)
pvals <- replicate(10000, {
  X <- generate_data(config)
  ece.test(X, type = "bs.parametric", B = 1000)$p.value
})
hist(pvals, breaks = 20, freq = FALSE,
     xlab = "p-value", main = "Null distribution of parametric bootstrap p-values")
abline(h = 1, col = "red", lty = 2)
mean(pvals < 0.1)
```
:::

**Consistency of $V$.** The parametric bootstrap is valid only if $V$ consistently estimates $\operatorname{Var}(\bar{S})$. If $V$ is systematically too small, the bootstrap null distribution will be too narrow, producing an excess of small p-values. We check this by simulating many datasets under $H_0$, computing the empirical variance of $\bar{S}$ across replications, and comparing it to the average of the estimated $V$. The two should agree.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Code: Consistency of $V$
```{R}
#| cache: true
config <- scenario(2, n = 1000, L = 2)

sims <- map(1:10000, ~ {
  X <- generate_data(config)
  n <- nrow(X)
  S <- ece_terms(X)
  list(
    S_bar = colMeans(S),
    W     = as.numeric(
      (1 / n^2) * (
        t(S) %*% S +
        t(rotate(S)) %*% S + t(S) %*% rotate(S) +
        t(rotate(S, 2)) %*% S + t(S) %*% rotate(S, 2)
      )
    )
  )
})

S_bar_vals <- map_dbl(sims, "S_bar")
W_vals     <- map_dbl(sims, "W")

bs_draws <- rnorm(10000, 0, sqrt(mean(W_vals)))

xr <- range(c(S_bar_vals, bs_draws))
hist(S_bar_vals, breaks = 40, freq = FALSE, col = adjustcolor("red",  0.4),
     xlim = xr, xlab = expression(bar(S)), main = "")
hist(bs_draws,   breaks = 40, freq = FALSE, col = adjustcolor("blue", 0.4), add = TRUE)
abline(v = c(-1, 1) * sd(S_bar_vals),        col = "red",  lty = 2)
abline(v = c(-1, 1) * sqrt(mean(W_vals)),    col = "blue", lty = 2)
legend("topright",
       legend = c(expression("empirical "*bar(S)), expression("N(0, "*bar(V)*")")),
       fill = adjustcolor(c("red", "blue"), 0.4), border = NA)
```
:::

## Theoretical Results

We want to characterize $W := \operatorname{Cov}(\bar S)$. Its general entry is $W_{(a,b),(c,d)} = \operatorname{Cov}\!\left(\bar S_{(a,b)}, \bar S_{(c,d)}\right)$, and by bilinearity,
$$W_{(a,b),(c,d)} = \frac{1}{n^2}\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^n \operatorname{Cov}\!\left(S_{i,(a,b)}, S_{j,(c,d)}\right).$$
Since $S_{i,(a,b)}$ depends only on $X_i, X_{i+1}, X_{i+2}$, this covariance is $0$ whenever $|i-j| \geq 3$ — the same bandwidth-2 structure used to build $V$ above — so only lags $m \in \{0,\pm1,\pm2\}$ survive.

The Theorem below gives each of these lag covariances in closed form under the null model $X_i = \theta_i + \varepsilon_i$, $\theta_i$ a deterministic piecewise-constant mean. Its main payoff: the covariance is exactly $0$ at every lag whenever $\{a,b\}$ and $\{c,d\}$ are disjoint, and generally nonzero otherwise (equal pairs, or one shared coordinate). This is the one fact we can actually exploit — it lets us mask out the disjoint-pair entries of $W$ as exactly zero, rather than estimate a quantity known in advance to vanish, cutting the free entries of $W$ from all $q \times q$ pairs down to those sharing at least one coordinate.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Theorem: Lag-0, lag-1, and lag-2 autocovariance

Assume the null model above, and take $a < b$, $c < d$.

**Lag 0.** When $(c,d) = (a,b)$,
$$\operatorname{Cov}\!\left(S_{i,(a,b)}, S_{i,(a,b)}\right) = \frac{5}{2}\sigma_a^2\sigma_b^2 + \frac{1}{2}\sigma_a^2(\theta_{i,b} - \theta_{i+2,b})^2 + \frac{1}{2}\sigma_b^2(\theta_{i,a} - \theta_{i+2,a})^2;$$
when $\{a,b\} \cap \{c,d\} = \{j\}$ with partners $r, s$ (i.e. $\{a,b\} = \{j,r\}$, $\{c,d\} = \{j,s\}$),
$$\operatorname{Cov}\!\left(S_{i,(a,b)}, S_{i,(c,d)}\right) = \frac{1}{2}\sigma_j^2(\theta_{i,r} - \theta_{i+2,r})(\theta_{i,s} - \theta_{i+2,s});$$
and the covariance is $0$ when $\{a,b\}$ and $\{c,d\}$ are disjoint.

**Lag 1.** When $(c,d) = (a,b)$,
$$\operatorname{Cov}\!\left(S_{i,(a,b)}, S_{i+1,(a,b)}\right) = \frac{1}{2}\sigma_a^2\sigma_b^2 + \frac{1}{2}\sigma_a^2(\theta_{i,b} - \theta_{i+1,b})(\theta_{i+2,b} - \theta_{i+3,b}) + \frac{1}{2}\sigma_b^2(\theta_{i,a} - \theta_{i+1,a})(\theta_{i+2,a} - \theta_{i+3,a});$$
when $\{a,b\} \cap \{c,d\} = \{j\}$ with partners $r, s$,
$$\operatorname{Cov}\!\left(S_{i,(a,b)}, S_{i+1,(c,d)}\right) = \frac{1}{2}\sigma_j^2(\theta_{i,r} - \theta_{i+1,r})(\theta_{i+2,s} - \theta_{i+3,s});$$
and $0$ when disjoint.

**Lag 2** (no quadratic part). When $(c,d) = (a,b)$,
$$\operatorname{Cov}\!\left(S_{i,(a,b)}, S_{i+2,(a,b)}\right) = -\frac{1}{4}\sigma_a^2(\theta_{i,b} - \theta_{i+1,b})(\theta_{i+3,b} - \theta_{i+4,b}) - \frac{1}{4}\sigma_b^2(\theta_{i,a} - \theta_{i+1,a})(\theta_{i+3,a} - \theta_{i+4,a});$$
when $\{a,b\} \cap \{c,d\} = \{j\}$ with partners $r, s$,
$$\operatorname{Cov}\!\left(S_{i,(a,b)}, S_{i+2,(c,d)}\right) = -\frac{1}{4}\sigma_j^2(\theta_{i,r} - \theta_{i+1,r})(\theta_{i+3,s} - \theta_{i+4,s});$$
and $0$ when disjoint.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Corollary: lag-2 vanishes when $L \geq 4$

Every lag-2 case above (equal pairs, one shared coordinate) is a product of two factors of the form $(\theta_{i,\cdot} - \theta_{i+1,\cdot})(\theta_{i+3,\cdot} - \theta_{i+4,\cdot})$. The first factor is nonzero only if $i$ is a change point ($\theta_i \neq \theta_{i+1}$); the second only if $i+3$ is. If both hold, some segment between them has length $\leq 3$, so under the minimum-segment-length assumption $\mathcal{L}(\theta) \geq L$ with $L \geq 4$ (i.e. $\theta \in \Theta_4$), the two factors can never both be nonzero. Combined with the disjoint-pair case, which is $0$ at every lag unconditionally, this means $\operatorname{Cov}(S_i, S_{i+2}) = 0$ identically once $L \geq 4$.

The sample-quantity term $S^\top C_2 S$ (and its transpose) in $V$ is then estimating a quantity known to be exactly zero, so it can be dropped without introducing bias:
$$V = \frac{1}{n^2} S^\top \left(I + C_1 + C_1^\top\right) S, \qquad L \geq 4.$$
:::

### Variations

Each variation below replaces part of $V$ with a value the Theorem pins to zero in advance. A sample term that estimates a known zero contributes only noise, so every entry we can pin is an entry we should not estimate.

Assume $\theta \in \Theta_L$. The Theorem's three cases then reduce to the following, where "quadratic" denotes the $\sigma_a^2\sigma_b^2$ contribution and "linear" the contributions carrying mean jumps:

| entry $W_{(a,b),(c,d)}$ | lag 0 | lag 1 | lag 2 |
|---|---|---|---|
| $(c,d) = (a,b)$ | quadratic $+$ linear | quadratic only ($L \geq 3$) | $0$ ($L \geq 4$) |
| $\{a,b\} \cap \{c,d\} = \{j\}$ | linear only | $0$ ($L \geq 3$) | $0$ ($L \geq 4$) |
| disjoint | $0$ | $0$ | $0$ |

Reading the table by column gives the lag-2 drop and the lag-1 diagonalization; reading it by row gives the mask.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Corollary: lag-1 is diagonal when $L \geq 3$

Every linear term at lag 1 (equal pairs and one shared coordinate alike) is a product of two factors of the form $(\theta_{i,\cdot} - \theta_{i+1,\cdot})(\theta_{i+2,\cdot} - \theta_{i+3,\cdot})$. The first is nonzero only if $i$ is a change point, the second only if $i+2$ is. If both hold, the segment between them — indices $i+1, i+2$ — has length $2$, so $\theta \in \Theta_L$ with $L \geq 3$ rules it out. Every lag-1 linear term therefore vanishes, leaving
$$\operatorname{Cov}\!\left(S_{i,(a,b)}, S_{i+1,(c,d)}\right) = \begin{cases} \frac{1}{2}\sigma_a^2\sigma_b^2, & (c,d) = (a,b), \\ 0, & \text{otherwise,}\end{cases}$$
since lag 1 has no quadratic part off the diagonal. So $\operatorname{Cov}(S_i, S_{i+1})$ is a diagonal matrix. This is implied by the $L \geq 4$ already assumed for the lag-2 Corollary.

Lag 0 is not diagonalized by the same argument: its shared-coordinate entry $\frac{1}{2}\sigma_j^2(\theta_{i,r} - \theta_{i+2,r})(\theta_{i,s} - \theta_{i+2,s})$ requires only *one* change point in the window, so no minimum segment length removes it.
:::

**`bs.parametric.lag1`** ($L \geq 4$). The lag-2 column is identically zero, so the $C_2$ terms are dropped:
$$V = \frac{1}{n^2}\, S^\top \left(I + C_1 + C_1^\top\right) S.$$

**`bs.parametric.mask`** (any $L$). The disjoint row is zero at every lag, unconditionally. Let $O_{(a,b),(c,d)} = \left|\{a,b\} \cap \{c,d\}\right|$ and let $M = \mathbf{1}\!\left[O > 0\right]$. Masking replaces the estimated disjoint entries with exact zeros,
$$V = \frac{1}{n^2}\, M \circ \left[S^\top \left(I + C_1 + C_1^\top + C_2 + C_2^\top\right) S\right],$$
cutting the free entries of $W$ from all $q \times q$ down to those sharing at least one coordinate. It composes with any of the other variations.

**`bs.parametric.lag1.diag`** ($L \geq 4$). By the Corollary the lag-1 column has a single nonzero case, so $\operatorname{Cov}(S_i, S_{i+1})$ is diagonal and every off-diagonal entry of $S^\top(C_1 + C_1^\top)S$ estimates zero. Keeping only its diagonal,
$$V = \frac{1}{n^2}\left(S^\top S + \operatorname{diag}\!\left[S^\top\left(C_1 + C_1^\top\right) S\right]\right).$$
This is `bs.parametric.lag1` with the lag-1 off-diagonals additionally pinned. The lag-0 component stays full.

**`bs.parametric.lag1.diag.mask`** ($L \geq 4$). Masking the remaining lag-0 component,
$$V = \frac{1}{n^2}\left(M \circ S^\top S + \operatorname{diag}\!\left[S^\top\left(C_1 + C_1^\top\right) S\right]\right).$$
Since $O_{(a,b),(a,b)} = 2$ always, $M$ alters only off-diagonal entries, while $\operatorname{diag}[\cdot]$ alters only the diagonal; the two act on disjoint entries and commute, so masking the lag-0 component is the same as masking the assembled $V$. Every entry of $V$ is now either pinned to zero or estimated by the one component of the table that contributes to it, which exhausts what the Theorem provides.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Remark: positive semi-definiteness

$V$ must be a valid covariance matrix to draw $S^{(b)} \sim N(0, V)$, and the truncated estimator $S^\top(I + C_1 + C_1^\top)S$ carries no such guarantee — this is the standard motivation for the Bartlett weights of Newey–West. The `.psd` variants repair it after the fact by clipping negative eigenvalues to zero.

`bs.parametric.lag1.diag` needs no repair. $S^\top S$ is a Gram matrix, hence positive semi-definite, and the entries of $\operatorname{diag}[S^\top(C_1 + C_1^\top)S]$ estimate $\sigma_a^2\sigma_b^2 > 0$, so the added diagonal is non-negative with probability approaching one; adding a non-negative diagonal preserves positive semi-definiteness. The structure supplies what the eigenvalue clipping was approximating.

Masking does not preserve positive semi-definiteness — zeroing off-diagonal entries of a PSD matrix generally destroys it — so `bs.parametric.lag1.diag.mask` may still require the `.psd` repair. The mask buys variance reduction on the disjoint entries, whose share grows with $p$, and pays for it through the clipping.
:::

### Computational Verification

We check the Theorem's disjoint-pair claim directly: for each of the $q \times q$ entries of $W$, simulate its sampling distribution across many replicates, and compare mutually exclusive (disjoint) pairs against pairs that share a coordinate. Disjoint pairs are highlighted in red and should concentrate near zero; the annotation in each panel gives the sample mean.

We use scenario 2 (square-wave mean shift) with $p = 5$ coordinates ($q = \binom{5}{2} = 10$ pairs), sample size $n = 1000$, and period $L = 4$, drawing 500 independent replicates of $X$.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| cache: true
p <- 5
params <- scenario(2, n = 1000, p = p, L = 4)
O <- pair_overlap(p)
labels <- colnames(O)
q <- length(labels)

sims <- map(1:500, ~{
  X <- generate_data(params)
  n <- nrow(X)
  S <- ece_terms(X)
  (1 / n^2) * (
    t(S) %*% S +
      t(rotate(S)) %*% S + t(S) %*% rotate(S) +
      t(rotate(S, 2)) %*% S + t(S) %*% rotate(S, 2)
  )
}, .progress = TRUE)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
idx <- expand.grid(i = 1:q, j = 1:q) |> filter(i <= j)

w_long <- imap_dfr(sims, ~{
  mutate(idx, rep = .y, value = .x[cbind(i, j)])
}) |> mutate(
  row_label = factor(labels[i], levels = labels),
  col_label = factor(labels[j], levels = labels),
  disjoint  = O[cbind(i, j)] == 0
)

panel_stats <- w_long |>
  summarise(mean = mean(value), .by = c(row_label, col_label, disjoint)) |>
  mutate(label = paste0("mean=", formatC(mean, format = "g", digits = 2)))

w_long |>
  ggplot(aes(x = value, fill = disjoint)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "firebrick", `FALSE` = "steelblue"), guide = "none") +
  geom_text(data = panel_stats, aes(x = Inf, y = Inf, label = label),
            hjust = 1.1, vjust = 1.5, size = 2.5, color = "black") +
  facet_grid(row_label ~ col_label, scales = "free") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL,
       title = "Residuals: estimated - theoretical",
       subtitle = "Red = mutually exclusive pairs (theoretical 0), annotation = sample mean") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9) +
  theme(axis.text = element_blank(), axis.ticks = element_blank())
```
